concepts.name: Dalton’s atomic theory
concepts.why: Dalton’s postulates say that matter is made of atoms, that the atoms of one element all have the same characteristic mass and differ from the atoms of every other element, that a compound holds atoms of two or more elements in a small, whole-number ratio, and that atoms are neither created nor destroyed in a chemical change but only rearranged. These postulates give a microscopic explanation of the macroscopic behavior of matter the reader has already met, including the conservation of matter, and every later picture of the atom starts from them.
concepts.evidence: The section lists the five postulates with Figures 2.2 to 2.4, and Example 2.1, its Check Your Learning and the first exercise ask whether a change drawn in colored spheres violates any of them.

concepts.name: The law of definite proportions
concepts.why: All samples of a pure compound contain the same elements in the same proportion by mass, which is what Dalton’s fourth postulate predicts if the numbers of atoms in a compound always stand in the same ratio. Note that the converse is not true: two samples with the same mass ratio are not necessarily the same substance.
concepts.evidence: Table 2.1 shows three samples of isooctane with the same carbon-to-hydrogen mass ratio of 5.33:1, and an exercise asks which postulate two samples of titanium dioxide of different composition would violate.

concepts.name: The law of multiple proportions
concepts.why: When two elements form more than one compound, a fixed mass of one element reacts with masses of the other in a ratio of small whole numbers. Taking the ratio of the two mass ratios is the step that reveals it, and atomic theory explains it at once, since one compound simply holds more atoms of one element per atom of the other.
concepts.evidence: The two copper chlorides of Figure 2.5 give a ratio of ratios of 2 to 1, and Example 2.2 and its Check Your Learning ask the reader to decide from mass data whether two compounds show definite or multiple proportions.

concepts.name: Thomson’s cathode rays and the electron
concepts.why: The beam in a cathode ray tube bends toward a positive charge and away from a negative one, is the same whatever metal the electrodes are made of, and has a charge-to-mass ratio showing its particles are far lighter than atoms. Thomson concluded that the particles are negatively charged subatomic constituents of all atoms, which is the first evidence that the atom is not indivisible.
concepts.evidence: The section argues from Figure 2.6 to Thomson’s conclusions, and an exercise asks how electrons and protons are alike and how they differ.

concepts.name: Millikan’s fundamental charge
concepts.why: The charge on every oil drop Millikan measured is a whole-number multiple of 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, so that value must be the charge of a single electron. Combined with Thomson’s charge-to-mass ratio, it gives the mass of the electron by a simple calculation.
concepts.evidence: Figure 2.7 tabulates the charges of five drops, and the section divides the electron’s charge by Thomson’s ratio to find its mass, 9.107 × 10⁻³¹ kg.

concepts.name: Rutherford’s nuclear atom
concepts.why: Most α particles pass straight through a gold foil, a few are deflected slightly and a very few bounce almost straight back. Rutherford reasoned that the atom must be mostly empty space with a small, heavy, positively charged nucleus at its center, which replaced both the plum pudding model and the Saturn-like model and is still the picture used today.
concepts.evidence: Figures 2.8 to 2.10 set the two earlier models beside the gold foil experiment and its explanation, and two exercises ask the reader to predict the paths of α particles fired at a plum pudding atom and at a Rutherford atom.

concepts.name: Protons, neutrons, and electrons
concepts.why: An atom is built from three kinds of subatomic particle: the negatively charged, very light electron outside the nucleus, and the positively charged proton and the uncharged neutron of nearly the same mass inside it. Everything the chapter says about atomic number, mass number, isotopes and ions is counted in these three particles.
concepts.evidence: The section introduces each particle with its discoverer, and exercises ask how protons and neutrons, and electrons and protons, are similar and how they differ; Table 2.2 in the next section gives their charges and masses.

concepts.name: Isotopes
concepts.why: Atoms of the same element can differ in mass while remaining chemically identical, because they have the same number of protons and different numbers of neutrons. The existence of isotopes is the reason Dalton’s second postulate had to be restated in terms of chemical properties rather than mass.
concepts.evidence: The section tells how Soddy recognized isotopes and how Chadwick’s neutron explained them, and an exercise asks which of Dalton’s ideas isotopes violate.

concepts.name: The atomic mass unit and the fundamental unit of charge
concepts.why: Atoms are so small that grams and coulombs are inconvenient, so their masses are given in atomic mass units, exactly one twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom, and their charges in units of the charge of one electron. On these scales a proton and a neutron each weigh about 1 amu and carry charges of 1+ and 0, and an electron weighs about 0.00055 amu and carries 1−.
concepts.evidence: The section defines the unified atomic mass unit, the dalton and the elementary charge, and Table 2.2 lists the charge and mass of each subatomic particle in both kinds of unit.

concepts.name: Atomic number and mass number
concepts.why: The atomic number is the number of protons in the nucleus and is the defining trait of an element; the mass number is the total number of protons and neutrons. Their difference is the number of neutrons, and in a neutral atom the atomic number is also the number of electrons.
concepts.evidence: The section defines both numbers and writes A − Z as the number of neutrons, and several exercises ask for the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons in given isotopes.

concepts.name: Ions, cations, and anions
concepts.why: When the numbers of protons and electrons in an atom are not equal, it carries a charge equal to the number of protons minus the number of electrons and is called an ion. An atom that gains electrons becomes a negatively charged anion, and one that loses electrons becomes a positively charged cation.
concepts.evidence: The section works the sodium cation and the oxide anion, and exercises ask for the symbol of an ion from its numbers of particles and charge.

concepts.name: Finding the numbers of protons, neutrons, and electrons in an atom or ion
concepts.why: Given an element’s atomic number, a mass number and a charge, the reader should be able to count the particles: the protons from the atomic number, the neutrons from the mass number less the atomic number, and the electrons from the protons less the charge. The same reasoning run backward gives the charge from the counts.
concepts.evidence: Example 2.3 counts the particles in an iodine anion, its Check Your Learning finds the charge of a platinum ion, and several exercises ask for the particles in isotopes used in medicine and in the diet.

concepts.name: Chemical symbols
concepts.why: A chemical symbol of one, two or three letters stands for an element or for one atom of it, whether the reader means a single atom or a jar full. Only the first letter is capitalized, which is why Co is cobalt and CO is carbon monoxide, and some symbols come from the element’s name in another language.
concepts.evidence: Figure 2.13 labels a jar of mercury Hg, Table 2.3 lists common elements and their symbols, and the section explains how new elements are named.

concepts.name: Writing and reading the symbol of an isotope or ion
concepts.why: The full symbol of an atom places the mass number as a left superscript, the atomic number as a left subscript (often omitted) and the charge as a right superscript on the element’s symbol. Reading and writing these symbols, and the equivalent names such as magnesium-24 or Mg-24, is how the book refers to a particular isotope or ion from here on.
concepts.evidence: Figure 2.14 labels the parts of the symbol, Table 2.4 gives the symbols of the isotopes of the first ten elements, and exercises ask the reader to write the symbol of an ion from its particles and charge.

concepts.name: Average atomic mass
concepts.why: The mass listed for an element in the periodic table is a weighted average over its naturally occurring isotopes, the sum of each isotope’s mass multiplied by its fractional abundance. That is why most atomic masses are not whole numbers, and it is important to understand that no single atom has the average mass: no boron atom weighs 10.8 amu.
concepts.evidence: The section computes the average mass of boron, Example 2.4 and its Check Your Learning compute the average masses of neon and magnesium, and exercises ask for the average masses of bromine and lithium.

concepts.name: Calculating isotopic abundances from an average mass
concepts.why: For an element with two isotopes, the fraction of one can be written as x and of the other as 1 − x, and the average mass equation then becomes one equation in one unknown. Solving it turns the average atomic mass back into the percent composition by isotope.
concepts.evidence: Example 2.5 finds the abundances of chlorine-35 and chlorine-37, its Check Your Learning those of the copper isotopes, and an exercise the boron abundances from Turkish and American ores.

concepts.name: Mass spectrometry
concepts.why: A mass spectrometer charges the atoms or molecules of a vaporized sample, deflects the ions through an electric or magnetic field by an amount that depends on their mass and charge, and records how many arrive at each mass-to-charge ratio. The height of each peak is proportional to the fraction of the ions at that ratio, so the spectrum reads off which isotopes are present and in what abundance.
concepts.evidence: Figure 2.15 shows the instrument and the mass spectrum of zirconium with five isotope peaks, and the chapter introduction uses the method to identify biomarkers in exhaled breath.

concepts.name: Molecular formulas
concepts.why: A molecular formula writes the symbols of the atoms in a molecule with subscripts giving how many of each there are. Many elements exist as molecules of their own, such as the diatomic H₂, O₂ and N₂ and the eight-atom S₈, and the formula of such an element differs from its symbol for that reason.
concepts.evidence: Figures 2.16 and 2.17 represent methane and sulfur, and exercises ask why the symbol of oxygen or of sulfur differs from the formula of its molecule.

concepts.name: A subscript is not a coefficient
concepts.why: A subscript counts the atoms bonded together in one molecule, while a number written in front counts separate units. H₂ is one molecule of two bonded atoms, 2H is two separate atoms, and 2H₂ is two molecules, four different things for four ways of writing hydrogen.
concepts.evidence: Figure 2.18 draws H, 2H, H₂ and 2H₂ side by side, and the section states the distinction in the paragraph before it.

concepts.name: Structural formulas and molecular models
concepts.why: A structural formula shows which atoms are connected to which, with lines for bonds; a ball-and-stick model shows the arrangement of the atoms in space, and a space-filling model shows their relative sizes. Each representation adds something the molecular formula leaves out.
concepts.evidence: Figures 2.16, 2.17, 2.20 and 2.21 show methane, sulfur, benzene and acetic acid in several of these representations, and exercises ask for formulas read off structural drawings.

concepts.name: Finding an empirical formula
concepts.why: An empirical formula gives the simplest whole-number ratio of the atoms or ions in a compound, found by dividing the subscripts of the molecular formula by their largest common factor. A molecular formula is always a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula, so acetic acid, C₂H₄O₂, and glucose share the empirical formula CH₂O.
concepts.evidence: The section derives the empirical formulas of acetic acid and benzene, Example 2.6 and its Check Your Learning ask for the formulas of glucose and metaldehyde, and several exercises ask for empirical formulas.

concepts.name: Isomers
concepts.why: The same atoms can be connected in different ways, so compounds with the same molecular formula can have different structures and different properties. Structural isomers differ in how the atoms are connected, as acetic acid and methyl formate do, and spatial isomers differ only in the orientation of the atoms in space, as the two mirror-image forms of carvone do.
concepts.evidence: Figures 2.23 and 2.24 show the two kinds of isomer, and an exercise asks for two molecules built from two carbons, six hydrogens and one oxygen and what their relationship is called.

concepts.name: The periodic law
concepts.why: The properties of the elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers. Mendeleev arranged the elements by atomic mass and used the pattern to predict elements not yet found, and by the twentieth century it was clear that atomic number, not mass, orders the table.
concepts.evidence: The section tells how Mendeleev’s predictions of gallium and germanium were confirmed, with his table in Figure 2.25, and states the modern law before the table of Figure 2.26.

concepts.name: Periods and groups
concepts.why: The modern periodic table arranges the elements in order of increasing atomic number in seven horizontal rows, called periods, and eighteen vertical columns, called groups, so that elements with similar properties fall in the same group. Each box gives the element’s atomic number, symbol and average atomic mass, and a mass in square brackets marks an element made only of radioactive isotopes.
concepts.evidence: Figure 2.26 is the table itself, and exercises ask the reader to find elements by group and by period.

concepts.name: Metals, nonmetals, and metalloids
concepts.why: Metals are shiny, malleable and ductile and conduct heat and electricity well; nonmetals are dull and conduct poorly; metalloids conduct moderately well and share properties of both. The three classes occupy regions of the periodic table, so an element’s position predicts its general properties.
concepts.evidence: Figure 2.26 shades the three classes, and exercises ask the reader to classify elements as metals or nonmetals using the table.

concepts.name: Main-group elements, transition metals, and the named groups
concepts.why: The groups 1, 2 and 13 to 18 hold the main-group elements, groups 3 to 12 the transition metals, and the two rows beneath the table the inner transition metals, the lanthanides and actinides. Several groups have names of their own, the alkali metals, alkaline earth metals, pnictogens, chalcogens, halogens and noble gases, and their members have similar chemical properties.
concepts.evidence: Figure 2.27 marks each family on the table, and exercises ask the reader to classify elements as main-group elements, transition metals or inner transition metals and to find the lightest and heaviest members of named groups.

concepts.name: Naming the group an element belongs to
concepts.why: Given an element, the reader should be able to find it in the periodic table and give the name of its group, and given a group name and a period, find the element. This is the fluency with the table that the next two sections rely on for predicting ions and naming compounds.
concepts.evidence: Example 2.7 and its Check Your Learning ask for the group names of eight elements, and exercises ask for the element that is a given kind in a given period.

concepts.name: Predicting the charge of a monatomic ion
concepts.why: Main-group metals tend to lose enough electrons to have as many as the preceding noble gas and form cations whose charge equals their group number, and nonmetals tend to gain enough electrons to match the next noble gas and form anions whose charge is the number of groups they lie to the left of the noble gases. The rule weakens toward the middle of the table, where metals such as iron and copper form ions of more than one charge.
concepts.evidence: Figure 2.29 gives the common charges across the table, and Examples 2.8 and 2.9 and their Check Your Learning items ask for the symbol and charge of an ion from its position or its particles.

concepts.name: Polyatomic ions and oxyanions
concepts.why: A polyatomic ion is a group of bonded atoms that carries an overall charge and acts as a single unit, and an oxyanion is one that contains oxygen. The book asks the reader to memorize the names, formulas and charges of the common ones, and the suffixes -ate and -ite and prefixes per- and hypo- mark more or fewer oxygen atoms.
concepts.evidence: Table 2.5 lists the common polyatomic ions with their related acids, and exercises ask the reader to name the ions in compounds such as ammonium carbonate.

concepts.name: Ionic bonds and covalent bonds
concepts.why: When electrons are transferred and ions form, the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions is an ionic bond; when electrons are shared and molecules form, the attraction between the nuclei and the shared pairs of electrons is a covalent bond. Compounds are classified as ionic or molecular by the bonds present in them.
concepts.evidence: The section defines both kinds of bond before dividing compounds into the two classes, and Figure 2.28 shows a sodium atom losing an electron to become a cation.

concepts.name: Ionic compounds
concepts.why: A metal combined with one or more nonmetals usually forms an ionic compound, a solid held together by ionic bonds that melts at a high temperature and conducts electricity when molten but not when solid. Its formula gives the relative numbers of ions rather than a molecule, since an ionic compound has no discrete molecules.
concepts.evidence: Figure 2.30 shows molten sodium chloride conducting, and the section explains why sodium oxalate is written Na₂C₂O₄ rather than as an empirical formula.

concepts.name: Writing the formula of an ionic compound
concepts.why: An ionic compound is electrically neutral, so its formula takes the ions in the ratio that makes the positive and negative charges equal, with a polyatomic ion treated as a unit in parentheses when more than one is needed. Two Al³⁺ and three O²⁻ give Al₂O₃, and one Ca²⁺ with two H₂PO₄⁻ gives Ca(H₂PO₄)₂.
concepts.evidence: Examples 2.10 and 2.11 and their Check Your Learning items predict four formulas, and exercises ask for the formula of the compound formed by each pair of ions.

concepts.name: Molecular compounds
concepts.why: Compounds of nonmetals usually consist of discrete, neutral molecules held together by covalent bonds, and under normal conditions they are often gases, low-boiling liquids or low-melting solids. The book notes that predicting this from positions in the periodic table is a simplistic approach with interesting exceptions.
concepts.evidence: The section contrasts molecular compounds with ionic ones and names aluminum chloride as an exception to the metal-and-nonmetal rule.

concepts.name: Predicting whether a compound is ionic or molecular
concepts.why: Given a formula, the reader should be able to find its elements in the periodic table and predict that a metal with nonmetals, or a compound with a polyatomic ion, is ionic, and that nonmetals alone form a molecular compound. It is the first question asked before naming any compound in the next section.
concepts.evidence: Example 2.12 and its Check Your Learning classify eight compounds, and exercises ask the reader to classify chlorides and other compounds and to write the ions of those that are ionic.

concepts.name: Naming ionic compounds
concepts.why: An ionic compound is named cation first and anion second: the metal’s name, then the nonmetal’s name with its ending replaced by -ide, or the name of the polyatomic ion as it stands. Because the charges fix the ratio of the ions, the name does not need to state how many of each there are.
concepts.evidence: Tables 2.6 to 2.8 give examples of binary and polyatomic ionic compounds and their everyday uses, and exercises ask the reader to name compounds and to write formulas from names.

concepts.name: Naming compounds of metals with variable charge
concepts.why: When a metal can form ions of more than one charge, the charge of its ion is worked out from the formula and the anion’s fixed charge and written as a Roman numeral in parentheses after the metal’s name, as in iron(II) chloride and iron(III) chloride. The older suffixes -ous and -ic for the lower and higher charges survive in some industries.
concepts.evidence: Table 2.9 lists variably charged metal compounds, Example 2.13 names five compounds, and exercises ask for IUPAC names of compounds such as ferric nitrate and cupric bromide.

concepts.name: Naming and writing formulas of ionic hydrates
concepts.why: A hydrate is named by adding to the name of the anhydrous compound a Greek prefix for the number of water molecules per formula unit followed by the word hydrate, and its formula appends a centered dot, that number and H₂O. Copper(II) sulfate pentahydrate is CuSO₄·5H₂O.
concepts.evidence: The section names copper(II) sulfate pentahydrate and sodium carbonate decahydrate with Table 2.10 of prefixes, and Example 2.13 and its Check Your Learning include a hydrate each.

concepts.name: Naming binary molecular compounds
concepts.why: Two nonmetals can combine in several ratios, so the name of a binary molecular compound gives the number of each atom with a Greek prefix: the more metallic element first, the other second with the suffix -ide, and mono- dropped from the first. CO is carbon monoxide and N₂O₄ is dinitrogen tetroxide.
concepts.evidence: Table 2.11 lists ten molecular compounds and their names, and Example 2.14 and its Check Your Learning ask for names and formulas of eight covalent compounds.

concepts.name: Naming binary acids
concepts.why: A compound of hydrogen and one other nonmetal dissolved in water is named as an acid by turning hydrogen into the prefix hydro-, adding -ic to the other element’s name, and adding the word acid, so that hydrogen chloride in water is hydrochloric acid.
concepts.evidence: Table 2.12 names five gases and the acids they form in water.

concepts.name: Naming oxyacids
concepts.why: An oxyacid is named from its oxyanion by omitting hydrogen, replacing -ate with -ic or -ite with -ous, and adding acid, so that H₂CO₃ is carbonic acid and HNO₂ is nitrous acid. Sulfuric and sulfurous acids are the book’s named exceptions.
concepts.evidence: Table 2.13 names eight oxyacids beside their anions, and an exercise asks for the formula of sulfuric acid.
